SD-Acc: Accelerating Stable Diffusion through Phase-aware Sampling and Hardware Co-OptimizationsThanks:  Zhican Wang and Guanghui He are with the State Key Laboratory of Micro-Nano Engineering Science, and School of Integrated Circuits, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, China (e-mail: {wang_zhican, guanghui.he}@sjtu.edu.cn). Hongxiang Fan is with Imperial College London, UK (e-mail:hongxiang.fan@imperial.ac.uk).

Zhican Wang, Guanghui He∗, Member, IEEE, Hongxiang Fan Affiliation: 
Abstract

The emergence of diffusion models has significantly enhanced the capabilities of generative AI, leading to improved quality, realism, and creativity in image and video generation. Among these, Stable Diffusion (StableDiff) become one of the most influential diffusion models for text-to-image generation, serving as a critical component in next-generation multi-modal algorithms. Despite their advances, StableDiff imposes substantial computational and memory demands, affecting inference speed and energy efficiency. To address these hardware performance issues, we identify three key challenges: 1) intensive and potentially redundant computation. 2) heterogeneous operators involving both convolutions and attention mechanisms. 3) widely varied weight and activation sizes.

Thus, we present SD-Acc, a novel algorithm and hardware co-optimization solution: At the algorithmic level, we observe that high-level features exhibit high similarity in certain phases of the denoising process, indicating the potential of approximate computation. Therefore, we design an adaptive phase-aware sampling framework to reduce the computational and memory requirements. This general framework automatically explores the trade-off between image quality and algorithmic complexity for any given StableDiff models and user requirements. At the hardware level, we introduce an address-centric dataflow to facilitate the efficient execution of heterogeneous operators within a simple systolic array. The bottleneck of nonlinear operations is comprehensively solved by our novel 2-stage streaming computing and reconfigurable vector processing unit. We further enhance hardware efficiency through an adaptive dataflow optimization that incorporates dynamic reuse and fusion techniques tailored for StableDiff, leading to significant memory access reduction. Across multiple StableDiff models, our extensive experiments demonstrate that our algorithm optimization can achieve up to 33 times reduction in computational demands while preserving the same level of image quality across various models. Together with our highly optimized hardware accelerator, our approach can achieve higher speed and energy efficiency over CPU and GPU implementations.

I Introduction

Recent advancements in diffusion models [16] have expanded the potential of AI-generated content (AIGC), enabling a wide range of applications, such as image editing, image super-resolution, and video synthesis. Among various AIGC applications, text-to-image generation, particularly through the use of Stable Diffusion (StableDiff) [49], has gained considerable attention for its ability to produce high-quality images based on user-provided textual prompts. Along with this popularity, deploying models on edge devices, such as personal computers and smartphones, to meet data privacy and model customization requirements is increasingly prioritized. However, the discrepancy between the limited resources of edge devices and the significant computational and memory demands of these models hinders their wider adoption [30, 38, 60].

To address the hardware performance challenges of these text-to-image models, previous research has primarily focused on minimizing computational demands and memory footprint at the algorithmic level, including efficient denoising sampling [34], knowledge distillation [39], pruning [10], and quantization [14]. Nevertheless, existing approaches suffer from several drawbacks. First, many of these algorithmic optimizations [39, 10, 14] typically require time-consuming retraining or fine-tuning processes, which require significant computational resources. Second, these methods primarily focus on algorithmic optimizations without considering the dataflow characteristics and execution efficiency of the underlying hardware. Consequently, it is challenging to translate the theoretical computation reductions into practical performance gains due to potential irregularities and workload imbalances.

To address the above limitations, this paper identifies three key challenges and proposes algorithm and hardware co-optimization to jointly improve the inference speed and energy efficiency of StableDiff.

At the algorithmic level, as shown in Fig. 1 (left), the generation process of StableDiff starts from the random noise. The model then iteratively generates new images with progressively less noise through a time-consuming denoising process, ultimately producing the target image. We identify the first challenge as long iterative timesteps with intensive and potentially redundant computation. To tackle this challenge, we first conduct a quantitative analysis of the activation distribution during the denoising process. Our analysis indicates that the denoising process can be divided into two distinct phases: sketching and refinement. This division into two phases is inspired by the human artistic painting process: sketching geometric contours and spatial arrangements, followed by focused refinement of local textures and details. During the sketching phase, statistical analysis reveals that both contextual and textural information vary significantly in diffusion models, warranting the retention of the complete sampling. Conversely, the refinement phase shows a stabilization in global and contextual information, with only local texture information undergoing active variation. The denoising process illustrated in Fig. 1 (left) supports this observation: the contour and sketch of the cat are largely determined after approximately half of the process. While many prior works, such as [38, 60, 25], have already identified the redundancy between consecutive timesteps, our unique motivation is that denoising from the sketch may require significantly fewer computations than denoising from scratch, but the steps after a half are equally significant that cannot be early terminated. Fig. 4 provides a more specific illustration, demonstrating the variation in information levels throughout the denoising process. The darker lines indicate higher-level information (sketch), while their magnitude represents the variation. It can be observed that all levels of information change dramatically at the beginning, akin to the sketching phase, while higher levels stabilize in the later phase, resembling the refinement phase. A more precise definition and quantitative analysis are provided in Sec. III-A. Motivated by this observation, we reuse features from the sketching phase and preserve only a minimal number of blocks during the refinement phase. This innovative method, termed phase-aware sampling, eliminates the need for retraining or fine-tuning while achieving significant computation reduction, maintaining comparable algorithmic performance to the original model. To generalize the proposed approach, we propose an optimization framework that dynamically adjusts hyper-parameters according to user constraints, enabling the exploration of the trade-off between hardware performance and image quality for various StableDiff models.

At the hardware level, previous co-designed accelerators are efficiently tailored for a specific algorithm but sacrifice generality, which restricts their applicability for general-purpose edge devices. To this end, our key focus is achieving efficiency while maintaining hardware simplicity and generality. Targeting StableDiff, efficient hardware support is required for both convolution and attention operations. However, existing dedicated accelerators are optimized for either CNNs or Transformers, but they fail to efficiently support both types of operations. Specifically, as shown in Fig. 1 (center), heterogeneous operators pose the second challenge. For linear operations, such as convolution and matrix multiplication (Matmul), current CNN accelerators [3, 4, 43] can efficiently support convolution but exhibit inefficiency in handling attention computations, and Transformer accelerators also lack the efficiency for convolution. Simply combining different engines may lead to hardware underutilization. An alternative solution is dataflow-flexible accelerators, such as [28, 46, 57]; however, this flexibility incurs significant overhead. For instance, [28] requires 47%47\% more area than a systolic array to efficiently support both convolution and Matmul. Another common solution is to use im2col to transform convolution into matrix multiplication, which has seen successful deployment in both industry [31, 18] and academia [11]. However, as reported in [11, 53], im2col in software can account for up to 30%30\% of the end-to-end latency and result in a significant increase in memory access. Placing a dedicated im2col hardware module can alleviate this issue. However, it still faces bank conflicts due to irregular memory access [53]. Additionally, frequent conversions between formats introduce explicit latency, which is further aggravated by varying feature map shapes, kernel sizes, and strides. As a result, an elegant and low-cost solution is still lacking.

For nonlinear operations, as widely reported [24, 58, 55, 42], although nonlinear operations such as softmax, layernorm, and GELU constitute a small portion of the overall operations, they contribute to up to 30% of latency on CPU/GPU platforms. This substantial latency is caused by two main inefficiencies: (i) Softmax and layernorm require multiple passes over the data, with each pass introducing significant latency (e.g., calculation of mean, variance, and normalization in layernorm), and (ii) they require that all related data be preloaded before computation, obstructing linear operations and presenting storage challenges. Prior works [24, 20, 6] adopt a store-then-compute strategy by fusing these nonlinear operations with preceding linear computations. Although this approach reduces off-chip access, challenges in data dependency (e.g. softmax), limited on-chip memory, and reduced parallelism can potentially degrade performance [24]. Another line of research focuses on designing specialized and efficient engines to approximately implement nonlinear operations [64, 55, 23]. However, although these circuits maintain accuracy for specific tasks, they may not perform as well in other scenarios. Moreover, dedicated engines are not flexible enough to support other nonlinear operations, and designing multiple specialized engines for various tasks can diminish overall efficiency.

To comprehensively and holistically solve the above issues, we employ a general-purpose systolic array (SA) as the computation core for uniform support for linear operations, achieving hardware simplicity and generality. For linear operations, we propose a reconfigurable vector processing unit to uniformly support various nonlinear operations with a single engine cost while maintaining accuracy. To enhance the hardware efficiency for linear operations, we propose an address-centric dataflow for convolution, which comprehensively mitigates memory irregularity and bandwidth bottlenecks due to convolution. With our enhancements, convolutions with various kernel sizes (1×11\times 1 and 3×33\times 3) and strides (11 and 22) presents in StableDiff are effectively supported, which enables SAs to efficiently support both convolution and attention operations with negligible extra overhead. For nonlinear operations, to tackle inefficiency-(i), we divide the softmax and layernorm operations into two distinct stages. We observe that softmax and layernorm consistently occur between the preceding (pre-) and succeeding (post-) Matmul stages, and the SA writes the results of the pre-Matmul and reads the operands of the post-Matmul in a streaming manner. Therefore, we insert these distinct stages into the mandatory data streaming process, which operate in parallel with SA computations. To resolve inefficiency-(ii), we propose tile-decoupled scheduling via mathematical transformations, enabling softmax/layernorm computation once the first tile is generated. Our solution effectively hides the latency of nonlinear operations, rendering them transparent to the Matmul process, which is termed as 2-stage streaming computing.

By further profiling the memory traffic of StableDiff, we observe the third challenge, as shown in Fig. 1 (right): StableDiff contains multiple downsampling and upsampling blocks, performing feature transformations across different resolutions and channel sizes, leading to widely varied computational and memory requirements across various blocks. Building upon the address-centric dataflow, tailoring specifically for StableDiff, we propose adaptive dataflow optimizations that apply dynamic reuse and fusion strategies across different layers to minimize off-chip access. In summary, we make the following contributions:

  • •

    We observe an interesting phase division phenomenon and propose a novel phase-aware sampling approach to reduce the amount of computation and memory required by StableDiff, achieving significant computational savings from an algorithmic perspective. (Sec. III)

  • •

    We propose a address-centric dataflow for convolution, as well as a novel 2-stage streaming computation technique for nonlinear operations, together with a reconfigurable vector processing unit. Through dataflow optimization, convolution and attention are uniformly and efficiently supported on a simple systolic array, with negligible overhead, achieving both generality and simplicity. (Sec. IV)

  • •

    We introduce the adaptive reuse and fusion method, which dynamically applies different reuse and fusion strategies to accommodate varying weight-activation proportions across layers, thereby minimizing off-chip access, and achieving specificity and adaptability tailored for StableDiff. (Sec. V)

II Background

II-A Preliminaries

Inspired by non-equilibrium thermodynamics [52], diffusion models employ a sequence of timesteps to gradually generate the target images via an iterative denoising mechanism. Starting from an initialized random noise 𝐱T\mathbf{x}_{T} sampled from a Gaussian distribution 𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈)\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}), diffusion models iteratively produce the target image 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0} through TT steps of denoising steps. At each timestep t−1t-1, the output 𝐱t−1\mathbf{x}_{t-1} is derived from a sampling function ℱ⁡(𝐱t,t,ϵθ​(𝐱t,t,e))\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t,\epsilon_{\theta}\left(\mathbf{x}_{t},t,e\right)), where ϵθ(.)\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{.}) represents a neural network to predict the noise and ee denotes the conditional embeddings. The specific form of ℱ(.)\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{.}) varies across different diffusion models.

Among various diffusion models, StableDiff [49] emerges as a leading text-to-image diffusion model due to its excellent algorithmic performance and efficiency. The inference of StableDiff consists of three parts: i) a text encoder that generates conditional embeddings ee based on users’ prompts, facilitating the adaptation to varied textual inputs, and ii) a network (eg. U-Net) to predict the noise and perform the iterative denoising process, iii) a variational autoencoder (VAE) to map pixels from latent space to image. These components work in a pipeline manner to produce high-quality images from textual descriptions.

To analyze the performance bottleneck of StableDiff, we perform profiling of three main components with respect to the number of parameters, operation counts, and latency performance on both CPU and GPU platforms. As shown in Fig. 2 (left), among the three modules, the U-Net parameters occupy a major portion with 860860 million parameters. Since U-Net requires multiple executions, while VAE and text encoder require only once, the MAC of U-Net far outweighs those of the text encoder and VAE. In various platforms, from Fig. 2 (right), it can be observed that the total inference time of StableDiff consumes minutes of latency even on the GPU, while the CPU is slower and can take up to ten minutes. This low latency motivates our dedicated hardware and algorithm optimizations. In terms of latency breakdown, U-Net accounts for nearly 100×100\times the latency of VAE, while the latency of the text encoder is minimal. Within U-Net, CNNs consume around 60%60\% of latency, and Transformers consume the rest. Due to the dominance of U-Net, this work focuses on studying the acceleration of U-Net, and optimize both CNNs and Transformers.

II-B Network Architecture of U-Net

As shown in Fig. 3, U-Net consists of cascaded downsampling and upsampling blocks (both indexed from top to bottom), with a middle block between them. Common upsampling and downsampling blocks further contain cascaded ResNet and Transformer blocks. The ResNet block consists of 3×33\times 3 convolution layers with skip connection and incorporates time embedding information. The Transformer block incorporates 1×11\times 1 convolution layers and attention layers to include text-encoded information. Some blocks are slightly different, for instance, the first downsampling block only contains one 3×33\times 3 convolution layer, the 4t​h,7t​h,10t​h4_{th},7_{th},10_{th} downsampling block consists solely of a downsampling operation, and the 4t​h,7t​h,10t​h4_{th},7_{th},10_{th} upsampling block includes an additional upsampling operation. Downsampling and upsampling operations realize resolution variation, while the others only vary the channel sizes. The downsampling operation is achieved by 3×33\times 3 convolution with a stride of 22, while the upsampling operation is achieved by nearest interpolation. The distinguishing feature of U-Net is the skip connection from the downsampling block to the upsampling block, which concatenates with the main branch along the channel and jointly serves as the input of the upsampling block.

III Algorithm Optimization

Our phase-aware sampling aims to explore approximate computations in a hardware-friendly manner, leveraging the similarities and distinct characteristics during different phases of diffusion models. Drawing inspiration from the human painting process, where the early phase involves outlining the skeleton followed by a focus on details in the later phase, we observe a similar principle in the denoising process, revealed by statistic analysis of U-Net (Sec. III-A). Subsequently, based on these observations, we define the phase division phenomenon and present a detailed sampling scheme in Sec. III-B, which efficiently reduces computational costs without the need for retraining or fine-tuning while preserving the image quality. Lastly, we provide an optimization framework in Sec. III-C to enable the customized exploration of the trade-off between speedup and image quality.

III-A Key Observations

The typical human painting process begins with the sketching phase, which involves drawing geometric contours and establishing spatial arrangements. This phase is followed by a refinement stage, where local textures and details are gradually inserted. These two phases demand different levels of attention and focus on distinct elements, motivating to explore: 1) whether the denoising process follows a similar two-phase approach, and 2) whether varying degrees of approximation exist within these distinct phases. To investigate these questions, we perform a quantitative analysis of the internal activations and predicted noise levels of U-Net, shown in Fig. 4.

We define the shift score to indicate the difference in the activations between two adjacent timesteps. The calculation of the shift score SS can be formulated as

Sti=‖Ati−At−1i‖2‖At−1i‖2​(t>0)\textstyle S^{i}_{t}=\frac{\|A^{i}_{t}-A^{i}_{t-1}\|_{2}}{\|A^{i}_{t-1}\|_{2}}(t>0) (1)

where AtiA^{i}_{t} represents the input activation from the main branch of the it​hi_{th} upsampling block at timestep tt and ∥.∥2\|.\|_{2} is the L2 norm function. To measure the variations of the shift score across denoising timesteps, it is necessary to choose a scheduler and specify the total number of timesteps. For this analysis, we randomly sample 100100 prompts from the PartiPrompts dataset [63] and generate 100100 images for each prompt using the 50-timestep scheduler [21]. Given that shift scores can differ in scale across various blocks, we employ min-max scaling to normalize each block’s scores to a uniform range of [0,1][0,1], where the same scaling is also applied to the noise across different denoising timesteps. Subsequently, the shift score is calculated for each block per timestep and averaged across different images. According to the profiling results presented in Fig. 4, we have the following two key observations, which have been extensively validated with various models and configurations. These observations motivate the finding of phase division and drive the exploration of phase-aware sampling (Sec. III-B).
Key Observation 1: U-Net experiences varying difference across distinct denoising timesteps. As shown in Fig. 4, most blocks exhibit the following pattern: the shift scores change dramatically at the beginning, rising and then falling in a wave-like manner, before stabilizing and experiencing a slight rise again near the end, indicating their proximity to the final target is nearly accomplished in the initial phase.
Key Observation 2: Specific blocks, such as block-1 and block-2, still exhibit high variance in the later denoising timesteps. This behavior indicates that the upper blocks of U-Net become important in later timesteps, supporting the hypothesis that StableDiff focus more on detailed texture information in the final phase, similar to humans. In contrast, spatial and contextual information initially undergoes substantial changes but then remains stable.

III-B Phase-aware Sampling

Phase Division: Based on the above observations, this work proposes to divide the denoising process into two distinct phases: sketching and refinement. Inspired by K-means clustering [13] (K=2K=2), the transition timestep DD between the two phases can be determined by sweeping the timesteps:

D∗=a​r​g​m​i​nD=1⋯T−2​∑t=0D(St¯−μ¯s​k​t)2+∑t=D+1T−1(St¯−μ¯r​e​f)2,\textstyle D^{*}=\underset{D=1\cdots T-2}{argmin}\ \sum_{t=0}^{D}(\bar{S_{t}}-\bar{{\mu}}_{skt})^{2}+\sum_{t=D+1}^{T-1}(\bar{S_{t}}-\bar{{\mu}}_{ref})^{2}, (2)

St¯\bar{S_{t}} represents the averaged shift score of the blocks except for the outlier curves. μ¯s​k​t,μ¯r​e​f\bar{\mu}_{skt},\bar{\mu}_{ref} stands for the mean St¯\bar{S_{t}} of the divided phases. Due to distinctive characteristics, the above equation finds the global optimal transition timestep to minimize the variance sum of the two phases. D∗D* is a meta-parameter obtained through the calibration phase, which will be introduced in Sec. III-C.

To explore approximate computation, we adopt different strategies for the two phases outlined in Sec. III-A. As shown in Fig. 5 (top), we define the parameter set {Ts​k​e​t​c​h,Tc​o​m​p​l​e​t​e,Ts​p​a​r​s​e,Ls​k​e​t​c​h,Lr​e​f​i​n​e}\{T_{sketch},T_{complete},T_{sparse},L_{sketch},L_{refine}\}, which can be categorized into spatial and temporal types. For the spatial parameters, Ls​k​e​t​c​hL_{sketch} and Lr​e​f​i​n​eL_{refine} represent the number of top blocks in the incomplete U-Net during the sketching and refinement phases, respectively. Ts​k​e​t​c​hT_{sketch}, Tc​o​m​p​l​e​t​eT_{complete}, and Ts​p​a​r​s​eT_{sparse} are temporal parameters, where Ts​k​e​t​c​hT_{sketch} refers to the duration of the sketching phase, Tc​o​m​p​l​e​t​eT_{complete} represents the number of timesteps reserved for the complete U-Net at the beginning, and Ts​p​a​r​s​eT_{sparse} indicates the sampling period of complete U-Net during the sketching phase. A smaller Ts​k​e​t​c​hT_{sketch} indicates more aggressive compression, but it must not be less than D∗D^{*} to ensure stability.

Specifically, during the sketching phase, when the shift scores are more significant and the predicted noise is large, we maintain complete runs of the entire U-Net for the first Tc​o​m​p​l​e​t​eT_{complete} timesteps. Then, for the remaining Ts​k​e​t​c​h−Tc​o​m​p​l​e​t​eT_{sketch}-T_{complete} timesteps of the sketching phase, we employ uniform sparse sampling, running the complete network every Ts​p​a​r​s​eT_{sparse} timesteps and executing only the first Ls​k​e​t​c​hL_{sketch} blocks for the other timesteps to improve speed. During the refinement phase, since only the topmost blocks exhibit high shift scores, as shown in Fig. 4, we retain these downsampling and upsampling blocks while pruning the execution of others. The detailed pruning process for both phases is illustrated in Fig. 5 (bottom). As shown in the right zoom-in subfigure, since the activation from the latest complete timestep is reused as the entry point for the retained blocks, which is close to the real value, the output approximately matches the real value. The number of retained blocks, Lr​e​f​i​n​eL_{refine}, is determined by the significance level of the shift score based on the profiling results and should be no less than the number of outlier blocks. Additionally, Ls​k​e​t​c​hL_{sketch} should be no smaller than Lr​e​f​i​n​eL_{refine}.

It is worth noting that layer skipping for StableDiff is not our proprietary contribution. Deepcache [38] also adopts block skipping, while Cacheme[60] specifically skips attention. However, they don’t consider phase awareness, and the parameters, such as Lr​e​f​i​n​eL_{refine} and Ls​k​e​t​c​hL_{sketch} are fixed, rather than determined adaptively using our framework (Sec. III-C).

III-C General Optimization Framework

As discussed in Sec. III-B, our proposed phase-aware sampling is defined by several hyper-parameters including {Ts​k​e​t​c​h,Tc​o​m​p​l​e​t​e,Ts​p​a​r​s​e,Ls​k​e​t​c​h,Lr​e​f​i​n​e}\{T_{sketch},T_{complete},T_{sparse},L_{sketch},L_{refine}\}. These parameters decide the trade-off between the speedup and image quality. To generalize our approaches to different StableDiff models and facilitate the exploration of performance trade-offs, we propose a framework to optimize these hyper-parameters according to users’ requirements.

To evaluate the MAC reduction, we build a cost function f⁡(l)f(l) that quantifies the computational overhead associated with running the first ll downsampling and upsampling blocks of U-Net. As presented in Fig. 6, we examine the MAC operation counts for each block within U-Net. The cost function, f⁡(l)f(l), is assigned as the cumulative computational ratio for the initial ll blocks and normalized by the total MAC computation of the entire network, which is depicted as the purple line in Fig. 6. Thus, the overall MAC reduction across all denoising timesteps can be formulated as:

M​A​Cr​e​d​u​c​e=T∑t=0T−1f⁡(lt),\textstyle MAC_{reduce}=\frac{T}{\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}f(l_{t})}, (3)

where ltl_{t} represents the number of running blocks at timestep tt. The primary objective of our framework is to maximize the MAC reduction in Equation (3) while ensuring the image quality meets user requirements.

Fig. 7 presents an overview of our framework. Inspired by the calibration phase in neural network post-training quantization [41], we also employ a calibration prompt dataset to optimize the hyperparameters offline. The calibration dataset is generated by randomly selecting 5%5\% of the targeted prompt dataset. The calibration process takes less than one hour on a V100 GPU, and we also find that D∗D^{*} is quite robust to the randomness of the prompt. Firstly, users specify the targeted model and datasets, model configurations, and the requirements of performance and image quality (Sec. VI-A). Secondly, the framework plots and analyzes the shift core curve to obtain the outliers and D∗D*, as described in Sec. III-A. The model parser analyses the model structure and the MAC breakdown to obtain the cost function. Thirdly, the framework conducts the solution search under the constraints, obtaining the feasible ones. Finally, the framework generates the images according to the solution and validates their quality. It outputs valid solutions, providing the solution with maximum MAC reduction. Following this four-step process, users can explore the trade-off between hardware performance and image quality tailored to their specific scenarios.

IV Unified Hardware Architecture

To uniformly support both convolution and attention, we propose an address-centric dataflow in (Sec. IV-A). Subsequently, as described in Sec. IV-B, we introduce our simple and general-purpose hardware architecture with the mapping solution. In Sec. IV-C, we introduce a novel 2-stage streaming computing strategy for nonlinear operators, and Sec. IV-D illustrate the corresponding reconfigurable hardware support.

IV-A Address-centric Reinterpretation

Notations and inefficiencies. Conventionally, convolution can be represented using a six-layer loop nest in Fig. 9 (right) assuming a batch size of one, with the notation P,Q,H,W,R,S,Ci​n,Co​u​tP,Q,H,W,R,S,C_{in},C_{out} depicted in Fig. 9 (left). We use capital letters to represent the loop border, and the lowercase to represent the variable in the corresponding dimension. However, as shown in Fig. 9 (right), the spatial dimensions and shift window manner lead to memory access irregularity, making it challenging to efficiently support convolution on a systolic array at negligible cost.

Overview. The aforementioned issues are addressed through address-centric re-interpretation. First, rediscover the source of irregularity in convolution compared to Matmul. A 3×33\times 3 convolution example is shown in Fig. 8 (left), it is evident that the multiplication and addition across the input channel are the same as the dot-product in the Matmul, whereas the additional addition within the window is unique to convolution. It is straightforward to decompose the convolution kernel into 1×11\times 1 kernels, and each 1×11\times 1 convolution operation becomes Matmul. Second, re-evaluate the address relationship between input and output. These 1×11\times 1 convolutions only generate a partial sum compared with the original form, we identify a simple address mapping scheme between the index of input (source of the partial sum) and the output activation (destination of the partial sum).

Re-interpretation. Take the most commonly used convolution, the same convolution as the example, it involves zero padding to ensure the same height and width between the input and output. The original h,wh,w dimensions are combined into one dimension ll and L=H​WL=HW, li​nl_{in} lo​u​tl_{out} denote the input and output activation. As shown in Fig. 8 (right), according to the different kernel positions in the original 3×33\times 3 convolution, address mapping differs correspondingly. For example, the center 1×11\times 1 kernel (denoted as 5) convolves with input activation a and generates the partial result, where this partial result should be added to output activation at the position A. Similarly, the partial result from b, c, d… should be added to B, C, D…. Due to the same index between source and destination, the address mapping can be summarized as l→ll\xrightarrow{}l. For kernel-4 in Fig. 8, it convolves with a, b, c, d…, and the partial result should be added to B, C, D, E…, and the address mapping is l→l+1l\xrightarrow{}l+1. The rest can be deduced similarly as shown in Fig. 8 (right). Notably, certain edges of the input don’t have corresponding output, necessitating detection and avoidance of addition for these edges, where we use a flag to denote these.

IV-B Mapping and Hardware Architecture

Storage Format and Address-centric Dataflow. We define a new storage format for the address-centric dataflow. Because the address mapping scheme absorbs cumbersome spatial information, the original spatial dimensions of input H,WH,W, and output P,QP,Q can be eliminated, and they can be uniformly merged into a single dimension LL. Consequently, all activations can be represented as (L,Ci​n)(L,C_{in}). Similarly, the spatial dimensions of weights, RR and SS, can be combined as F=R​SF=RS, resulting in weight storage as (F,Co​u​t,Ci​n)(F,C_{out},C_{in}). As a result, our proposed dataflow can be represented using a simplified four-layer loop nest, which incorporates matrix multiplication and partial sum addition. The transformed dataflow is summarized in Fig. 10 (right), the entire process is referred to as an operator, Uni-conv. Lines 2-8 correspond to matrix multiplication with the size (Li​n,Ci​n)×(Ci​n,Co​u​t)→(Li​n,Co​u​t)(L_{in},C_{in})\times(C_{in},C_{out})\xrightarrow{}(L_{in},C_{out}). The outermost loop in Line 1 denotes the partial sum addition across each 1×11\times 1 kernel. Crucially, matrix multiplication can be performed in parallel with the partial sum addition of Line 9, effectively hiding latency.

Hardware Overview. As depicted in Fig. 10 (left), our architecture consists of a weight-stationary systolic array for Matmul, on-chip buffers, and a vector processing unit (VPU) for partial sum addition and nonlinear operations, which will be introduced in the next sections. The address generator produces the incremental address based on the base address and the stride configured to realize the address mapping scheme. The systolic array has a height and width of H,WH,W, (irrelevant to the size of input activation), while the VPU also has a height of HH, i.e., H−H- parallel. Transformers are supported by mapping matrix multiplication on the systolic array, and nonlinear operations on the VPU concurrently. Given the conflict between the limited size of the systolic array and input/weight/output buffers, and the extensive workload demands of a neural network, tiling becomes necessary. We denote the tiled workload mapping using L0,Ci​n0,Co​u​t0L^{0},C_{{in}}^{0},C_{{out}}^{0} to represent the tile size. In CNNs, the output activation of one layer becomes the input activation of the subsequent layer. Thus, we set Ci​n0=Co​u​t0C_{{in}}^{0}=C_{{out}}^{0} and H=WH=W.

Mapping. Fig. 10 (center) illustrates the mapping of one matrix multiplication, corresponding to Lines 2-8 in Fig. 10 (right). The loops in Lines 3 and 6 are spatial-for, while those in Lines 1-2 are temporary-for. Concerning the weight, each 1×11\times 1 kernel, sized (Co​u​t0,Ci​n0)(C_{{out}}^{0},C_{{in}}^{0}), is spatially mapped to the height HH and width WW of the systolic array, respectively, and stored in the weight registers. For input activations with dimensions (L0,Ci​n0)(L^{0},C_{{in}}^{0}), L0L^{0} is temporarily mapped, while Ci​n0C_{{in}}^{0} is spatially mapped to the width WW. Similarly, the output activation has dimensions (L0,Co​u​t0)(L^{0},C_{out}^{0}), with L0L^{0} temporarily mapped and Co​u​t0C_{{out}}^{0} spatially mapped to the height HH. Each matrix multiplication yields partial results. To implement Lines 1 and 9 in Fig. 10 (right), the VPU initiates the addition of partial sums and updates the results. In each cycle, Co​u​t0C_{out}^{0} results form a vector and flow out of the systolic array in parallel. Simultaneously, the VPU retrieves the previous Co​u​t0C_{{out}}^{0} partial results from the output buffer using addresses provided by the address mapping scheme, adds the newly generated result to them, and writes the latest addition result back to the output buffer. Notably, an address detector precedes the addition to exclude contributions from certain edges that do not affect the output. Upon completion of the matrix multiplication related to the last 1×11\times 1 kernel, the partial results become the final result. In addition, the stride-22 convolution in StableDiff is conveniently supported by changes in the input stride configuration from 11 to 22 or W+2W+2 when spanning rows.

Benefits. The address-centric dataflow and mapping have the following advantages. 1) Memory regularity: the dimension ll increases monotonically for both input and output, ensuring that bandwidth is efficiently utilized and equally distributed between them. 2) High PE utilization: the mapping ensures high PE utilization for nearly all U-Net layers, except for the first and last convolutions, which have small Ci​nC_{in} and Co​u​tC_{out}. However, their impact on latency is less than 1%1\%, which does not affect overall performance. 3) Simplicity and generality: convolution operations are efficiently managed by a naive systolic array, and the address mapping scheme can be easily implemented by adjusting the address bias of the output, with negligible overhead. 4) Compatibility: the dimension ll of convolution aligns well with the sequence length dimension of attention, which avoids any format conversion overhead, making the unified support for convolution and attention highly effective. Thus, the remaining challenge is addressing the bottleneck of nonlinear operations.

IV-C Latency Hiding of Nonlinear Operations

Motivations. Nonlinear operations are indispensable for model inference, but they can even consume up to 30%30\% latency on GPU/CPU platforms [24, 58, 55, 42]. This issue is more challenging in edge devices due to limited hardware resources. The bottleneck of nonlinear operations, such as softmax and layernorm arises from two inefficiencies: (i) They require multiple passes over the data (e.g., calculation of mean, variance, and normalization), with each pass introducing extra latency. Since they occur between Matmuls, this latency can block subsequent GEMV computations. (ii) They require all data to be available before computation begins and prevent parallel computation until all required data is available. This stalled latency degrades the systolic array utilization, hence, we propose a 2-stage streaming computing strategy to address this issue, as illustrated in Fig. 11 (a), where the comparison shows significant improvements.

Observations and Optimizations. Our approach builds on three key observations and optimizations. First, when evaluating the structure of these operations, softmax and layernorm can be split into two stages: numerical characteristic acquisition (NCA) and element-wise normalization (Norm), as illustrated in Fig. 11 (b). Second, these operations occur between matrix multiplication (Matmul) operations. Since systolic arrays generate results and read operands in a streaming fashion, it allows us to hide NCA and Norm latencies within the data streaming. Thus, as shown in Fig. 11 (c), we schedule the NCA stage concurrently on the VPU with the preceding (pre-) matrix multiplication and insert the computation pipeline before the multiplication results are written to the buffer, enabling simultaneous NCA. Similarly, the Norm stage is scheduled on the VPU only whenever the posterior (post-) matrix multiplication is needed. The computation pipeline is inserted after the operand is read from the buffer, preparing normalization results concurrently.

Tile Decoupling. These two steps address inefficiency-(i), while inefficiency-(ii) is resolved by our mathematical transformation. Layernorm is transformed as shown in Equation (4), allowing the sum and square sum to be computed concurrently with the preceding matrix multiplication results, and the mean and variance can be calculated immediately after the matrix computation finishes. However, softmax requires a global maximum to avoid numerical overflow. Inspired by [40], we compute a partial exponential sum using the current maximum in advance, which is updated as new tiles are generated. As shown in Equation (5), E​SES represents the exponential partial sum of N1N_{1} elements based on the previous global maximum (p​r​e​_​m​a​xpre\_max), while E​SnES_{n} is the partial sum of N0N_{0} elements from the new tile with the latest global maximum (n​e​w​_​m​a​xnew\_max). Each time a tile of size N0N_{0} is generated, as shown in Equation (6), we update E​SES, increment N1N_{1} by N0N_{0}, and simultaneously update the previous global maximum with n​e​w​_​m​a​xnew\_max. Based on these, our tile decoupled scheduling is shown in Fig. 11 (d), where the VPU operates concurrently with generating tiled results from the SA during the NCA stage and prepares operand reads for the SA in the Norm stage. In the NCA stage of softmax, due to the tile-based maximum search, the VPU completes the computation with a slight delay of tile latency. For Norm, the VPU should be scheduled in advance to account for pipeline latency. For layernorm, both the NCA and Norm stages incur pipeline latency. It is worth noting that the only extra end-to-end latency is either tile or pipeline latency, both of which are negligible.

Discussion. Furthermore, compared with previous works employ a store-then-compute strategy [24, 20], layernorm fusion requires all input data prepared and stored on the scratchpad, which restricts the Matmul tiling due to the limited scratchpad size, even possibly hurting the performance due to inefficient tiling [24]. In contrast, with our 2-stage streaming computing, data can even move to off-chip, since their characteristics have been stored immediately in the NCA stage. Due to efficient streaming, nonlinear operations are decoupled from Matmul, imposing no restrictions on storage or tiling.

IV-D General Reconfigurable VPU for Nonlinear Operations

Motivations. There is substantial work on designing specialized and efficient engines to approximately implement nonlinear operations [64, 55, 23]. However, this approach has limitations. First, while these circuits maintain accuracy for specific tasks, they may not perform as well in other scenarios. For example, I-GELU[23] performs well with BERT[8] but shows a significant performance degradation for StableDiff in our experiments. Second, dedicated engines are not flexible enough to support other operations, and designing multiple specialized engines for various operations can reduce overall efficiency.

Overview. To uniformly support various nonlinear operations, we design a reconfigurable arithmetic and special function array of the VPU in Fig. 10. This module comprises a comparator array, an exponential (EXP) array, a multiplier array, a divider array, two adder arrays, an ALU, and sufficient multiplexers. All arrays are H−H-parallel, with each row handling a single softmax or layernorm operation independently. The ALU is equipped with a register stack to store numerical characteristics. Since the entire input generates only two characteristics: exponential summation (e​x​p​_​s​u​mexp\_sum) and global maximum (x​m​a​xxmax) for softmax, mean and variance for layernorm, the storage cost is negligible.

Softmax Datapath. As shown in Fig. 12 (a) and Equation (5) (right), in the NCA stage with H−H- parallel independent rows of data streams in, each input xix_{i} enters a comparator and FIFO, where the FIFO depth is consistent with the tile size (e.g., 3232). The comparator consists of two registers: the first continuously tracks the latest maximum, while the second is only updated by the latest maximum once a new tile has been entirely stored in the FIFO, and it represents the current maximum (n​e​w​_​m​a​xnew\_max) for exponential accumulation. Once the FIFO is fully filled, it outputs and receives data simultaneously. The output subtracts n​e​w​_​m​a​xnew\_max, enters the EXP unit, and is then accumulated. If the element is the first of a tile, the accumulation register is directly set as its value, eliminating the need for a clear cycle. The process is controlled under the ALU counter. Due to the naturally skewed data of the systolic array as shown in figure leftmost, ALU is reused row-by-row to implement cross-tile e​x​p​_​s​u​mexp\_sum updating, as described in Equation (6). In the Norm stage, each element subtracts the final maximum x​m​a​xxmax, enters the reused EXP unit, and is divided by the final e​x​p​_​s​u​mexp\_sum. Layernorm Datapath. As shown in Fig. 12 (b), in the NCA stage based on Equation (4), the sum and square sum are accumulated in parallel by two adder arrays, and the square sum computing requires the data multiplied by itself using the multiplier array. In the NCA stage, ALU conducts the mean and variance computing using the sum and square sum and performs the square root computation, which is again one-by-one reused among each row due to the skewed input for the systolic array. Finally, adder and division arrays are utilized for the normalization. In GELU Datapath. The official sigmoid version of GELU is implemented in our hardware [15], which has been validated to show negligible accuracy loss for StableDiff. As shown in Fig. 12 (c), the FIFO is reused to buffer and delay operands, while the EXP, adder, multiplier, and divider arrays are configured to reuse for computation.

V Adapative Dataflow Optimization

The U-Net in StableDiff integrates different upsampling and downsampling blocks, leading to substantial variations in weight and activation sizes across layers. This poses a challenge in maximizing data reuse and minimizing memory access, which will be discussed in Sec. V-A. Therefore, we propose an adaptive dataflow optimization in Sec. V-B.

V-A Varied Weight and Activation Sizes

Observations. The sizes of weight and input activation of 3×33\times 3 convolution across the entire U-Net are shown in Fig. 13 (left) (center), indexed by 0−510-51. Both activations and weights vary significantly, with the weight size nearly reaching 30M in certain layers. However, we observe an interesting phenomenon: in the shallowest and deepest layers, activations are large while weights are small, whereas in middle layers, activations are small but weights are large. Consequently, we plot the curve of the minimum size of input and weight across the layers, as shown in Fig. 13 (right). It can be concluded that: 1) For the minimum size, most layers are below a threshold, denoted by the red line. This inspires us to leverage the hybrid reuse methodology to minimize the off-chip memory traffic. 2) For middle layers, their minimum size is determined by the activation, and they are much smaller, as indicated by the green line. This inspires us to keep both the entire input and output on-chip and utilize fusion techniques for these layers.

V-B Adaptive Reuse and Fusion Methodology

Based on the address-centric dataflow, it comprises (Li​n,Ci​n)×(Ci​n,Co​u​t)→(Li​n,Co​u​t)(L_{in},C_{in})\times(C_{in},C_{out})\xrightarrow{}(L_{in},C_{out}) matrix multiplications. Due to the limited global buffer size, tiling can be performed as Li​n=Li​n1∗Li​n0L_{in}=L_{in}^{1}*L_{in}^{0}, where Li​n0L_{in}^{0} represents the tile size, Li​n1L_{in}^{1} denotes the number of tiles, and the tiling notation of Co​u​tC_{out} and Ci​nC_{in} follows that. The design space is significantly simplified to a straightforward three-layer loop nest in Fig. 14, and we employ the following strategies. Considering a single layer: For layers with small input activations and large weights, the input is small enough to be stored in the global buffer. We reuse it with the related weight tiles along the Co​u​tC_{out} dimension, as shown in Fig. 14 (a), and Uni-conv refers to Fig. 10 (right). For layers with large input activations and small weights, weight is reused in the global buffer and utilized with the related input tiles along the Li​nL_{in} dimension, as shown in Fig. 14 (b). Through this adaptive reuse, for most layers, their input activations and weights can be accessed from off-chip only once. For the very few layers with both large weights and input activations, both of which exceed the global buffer, we can divide this layer into tiles. In summary, we consistently select the reuse method with less memory access for each layer.

Considering multiple layers: As shown in Fig. 14 (c) (top), the input and output activations in the middle layers are relatively small enough to store both on-chip. Once one layer is fully processed, the activation is directly forwarded to the next layer, which is layer-by-layer fusion. This approach can be applied to input or weight reuse, but it requires prioritizing buffer allocation for activations, which may lead to increased memory access of weight. For the shallowest and deepest layers, as shown in Fig. 14 (c) (bottom), the smaller weights make weight reuse feasible and enable the generation of streaming partial activations. Partial activations can be directly fed into the next layer’s execution before the entire activation is complete, eliminating off-chip access to intermediate activations, which is cross-layer fusion. As this method requires the entire channel to be computed, it is only compatible with weight reuse. The weights of the fused layers must be stored on-chip simultaneously, which may exceed buffer capacity and result in more weight access, thus, the number of layers to be fused should be carefully selected. Particularly, after determining reuse, the fusion method should first be decided for input-reuse layers, as they can only utilize layer-by-layer fusion or no fusion, followed by the decision for weight-reuse layers.

VI Evaluation

VI-A Experiment Setup.

Algorithm setup. We select StableDiff v1.41.4, v2.1−b​a​s​e2.1-base, and StableDiff XL as our targeted models because they are representative, influential, and open-source. For StableDiff v1.41.4, v2.1−b​a​s​e2.1-base, their latent resolutions are 64×6464\times 64, which generates images with size 512×512512\times 512. For StableDiff XL, its latent resolution is 128×128128\times 128, and the generated images are 1024×10241024\times 1024. The classifier-free guidance scale is set to the default value of 7.57.5. We use the PNDM scheduler [33] with a total of 5050 timesteps for sampling. We benchmark our method using the MS-COCO dataset validation split [32]. This dataset contains human-generated captions for images. We randomly sample 50005000 captions from it as the prompt input for StableDiff, thus generating 50005000 images with one prompt per image. Following popular settings [49, 48], each generated image is downsampled to 256×256256\times 256 resolution for metrics evaluation. We employ the CLIP score with the ViT-g/14 model to evaluate the correspondence between the images and prompts, where higher scores indicate better performance. We compute the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID), indicating distributional differences between the generated images and the ground-truth real-world images, and the inception score (IS) to assess image quality.

Hardware implementation. We utilize SystemVerilog and Vivado 2018.3 to synthesize and implement the hardware modules using the VCU118 Xilinx FPGA. The systolic array has a size of 32×3232\times 32, the vector processing unit is 32−32- parallel, and the arithmetic for the hardware is fp16. The hardware details are listed in Table I. Our energy consumption contains the on-chip cost and off-chip access, and the latter is derived from the access behavior and based on  [45]. We also adopt a cycle-accurate performance model to measure latency and memory traffic.

Baselines. For algorithm evaluation, we conduct the comparison with the original 5050 timesteps original model. To compare with the state-of-the-art works, Deepcahe [38] and BK-SDM [22] are selected because they are excellent open-sourced designs, optimizing the U-Net for StableDiff as well. Deepcache also utilizes layer skipping and BK-SDM employs the knowledge distillation. For hardware evaluation, we compare our design with the AMD Ryzen 7 6800H CPU, Intel(R) Xeon(R) Gold 5220R CPU, and NVIDIA V100 GPU. Additionally, we also conduct the ablation study to evaluate the gain of the address-centric adaptive dataflow optimization.

VI-B Algorithm Evaluation

Evaluation of various configurations. Our phase-aware sampling (PAS) is adequately evaluated with various configurations. As shown in Table II, the original model requires 5050 timesteps execution of the complete U-Net. In our phase-aware sampling, we change the Ts​p​a​r​s​eT_{sparse} and fix other hyper-parameters to test the image quality and MAC reduction. Across three different models, Ts​k​e​t​c​hT_{sketch} is set as 2525, as denoted by ’−25-25’, and Ls​k​e​t​c​h=Lr​e​f​i​n​e=2L_{sketch}=L_{refine}=2. For StableDiff v1.41.4, Tc​o​m​p​l​e​t​eT_{complete} is set as 44, while for the others Tc​o​m​p​l​e​t​e=3T_{complete}=3. Ts​p​a​r​s​eT_{sparse} is represented by ’/⁣∗/*’. For instance, /4/4 represents executing the complete U-Net once out of every four timesteps in the sketching phase. Our method achieves explicit MAC reduction for all the models. For image quality, we achieve CLIP scores similar to those of the original model. Interestingly, we achieve better FID and IS scores in some configurations. It may be because our method incorporates prior human knowledge, which has a regularization effect. This prevents the model from overfitting to the training datasets, making generated images closer to the real world. The effectiveness of the experimental result further demonstrates the p​h​a​s​e−d​i​v​i​s​o​nphase-divison phenomenon. As the MAC reduction increases, the CLIP score decreases and degrades the image quality, indicating the upper bound of MAC reduction.

Comparison with the state-of-the-art work. We select StableDiff v1.41.4 for comparison. As shown in Table III, our method outperforms BK-SDM and Deepcache in both inference performance and image quality. BK-SDM [22] compresses the U-Net by employing block pruning and feature distillation of the U-Net, resulting in MAC reduction and structured network architecture. However, their knowledge distillation requires retraining and may lead to overfitting, as indicated by the poor FID. Deepcache [38] adopts layer-skipping uniformly, but it does not realize the mechanism of phase division. In contrast, our method utilizes phase division to perform an adaptive sampling scheme without the need for retraining. Our general framework also allows for exploring the trade-off between image quality and acceleration.

VI-C Hardware Ablation Study

In this subsection, we focus on the FPGA inference of the original dense model, and select StableDiff v1.41.4 as a typical case to conduct an ablation study for each hardware optimization.

2-stage Streaming Computing Study. Since the latency of nonlinear operations is related to the sequence length and the hidden dimension of the Transformer, we extract different Transformer layers to study the effect of 2-stage streaming computing, with self-attention and FFN analyzed separately. These layers are labeled as −1-1, −2-2, and −3-3, with sequence lengths (i.e., feature map resolutions) of 40964096, 10241024, and 256256, respectively. The baseline shares the same hardware settings as the optimized solution, except for the use of 2-stage streaming computing. As demonstrated in Fig. 15 (left) for self-attention, our optimization nearly eliminates the entire latency of softmax, achieving latency reductions of 39%39\%, 24%24\%, and 14%14\%, respectively, compared with the baseline. The effect is more pronounced for larger sequence lengths, as the softmax operations scale quadratically. For FFN, as shown in Fig. 15 (right), our solution achieves latency reductions of 25%25\%, 14%14\%, and 8%8\%. The reduction is smaller because compared to the heavy matrix multiplications of the FFN, layernorm occupies a smaller portion of the computation. The savings are due to 2-stage streaming computing, on one hand, it avoids multiple passes of the data, improving memory efficiency, and on the other hand, absorbs computation into the data streaming of the systolic array’s read and write operations. Additionally, it decouples data dependencies and eliminates systolic array idleness caused by bottlenecks from nonlinear operations.

Adaptive Dataflow Optimization Study. Various operators are uniformly supported by the systolic array through address-centric dataflow, and our adaptive reuse and fusion optimization can further reduce off-chip access. To analyze the effect of this technique, we set the baseline with a systolic array of the same size, equipped with an im2col hardware module, following the design in  [11, 18]. The baseline is also equipped with streaming computing for nonlinear operations, and it has a global buffer of 22MB and a memory bandwidth of 38.438.4 GB/s, identical to the optimized solution for fairness. In our dataflow optimization, we dynamically employ the most suitable reuse scheme with less access between input and weight reuse, adapting to the varying weight and activation ratio across convolution layers. For most layers, input, weight, and output are accessed from off-chip only once by adaptive reuse, and fusion also avoids repeated input and output activation access. Considering all layers, adaptive reuse and fusion save 24.3%24.3\% and 30.5%30.5\% of off-chip access in total, respectively.

In more detail, as shown in Fig. 16 (left), cross-layer fusion is employed for layers 0∼50\sim 5 and 44∼5144\sim 51. Because for these layers, the activation size is large and the weight is small, we can reuse the weight on-chip and fuse the activations part by part, as mentioned in Fig. 14 (c). Due to the large activation sizes, the savings are evident. Layer-by-layer fusion is employed for layers 6∼366\sim 36 because the input and output activations of these layers are small and weights are large, making storing both activations in the global buffer feasible. However, due to the large weight size proportion, the reduction ratio is relatively smaller. For other layers, no fusion is adopted because we find that the increment of weight access surpasses the reduction of activation. Through this adaptive reuse and fusion, we not only reduce power consumption by minimizing memory access but also save bandwidth to enhance performance. Additionally, utilizing the optimization, the influence of global buffer size is explored as shown in Fig. 16 (right), and the off-chip access with the global buffer of 256256KB is normalized to one. The global buffer of 22MB is observed to achieve the sweet spot, while a larger buffer leads to higher costs and lower buffer utilization.

VI-D Technique Breakdown Analysis

In this subsection, we put the algorithmic and hardware optimizations together on the FPGA platform to analyze the speedup and energy efficiency improvement of each technique for StableDiff v1.41.4 as a typical case.

Roofline Model Analysis. As shown in Fig. 17 (a), the roofline model indicates that the inference of the StableDiff series on our FPGA platform (with a peak throughput of 204.8204.8 GFLOPS and a bandwidth of 38.438.4 GB/s) is compute-bound. Through phase-aware sampling, operational intensity increases because the timesteps executing only the topmost U-Net blocks are performed on the large resolution, providing more opportunities for convolution kernel reuse compared to the blocks below. Similarly, the Transformers in these top blocks also have longer sequence lengths. As a result, with more aggressive compression (larger Ts​p​a​r​s​eT_{sparse}), the averaged workload becomes increasingly compute-bound. Through our hardware optimizations, our solution significantly improves real throughput, bringing it close to the theoretical maximum.

Speedup Analysis. The effects of hardware and algorithmic optimizations are shown in Fig. 17 (b), left and right. For hardware optimization, we break down latency into memory access, systolic array computation, and others, which include nonlinear operations, im2col operations, and other minor latencies. The baseline consists of a systolic array equipped with an im2col module, following the design in  [11], and the latency is normalized to 11. Our hardware optimizations include address-centric dataflow (AC.), adaptive dataflow optimization (AD.), and 2-stage streaming computing (SC.). As shown in Fig. 17 (b) left, compared to the im2col implementation, the address-centric dataflow implementation achieves a 1.24×1.24\times speedup. This speedup is due to the original im2col operation causing irregular memory access and potential bank conflicts, whereas address-centric dataflow maintains regular memory access and effectively utilizes bandwidth. Furthermore, the im2col module introduces explicit latency, which can bottleneck systolic array computation, especially when the kernel, feature map size, and convolution stride vary. After applying adaptive dataflow optimization, our solution achieves a 1.37×1.37\times speedup over the baseline, due to reduced memory access and improved systolic array PE utilization. Finally, 2-stage streaming computing effectively hides the latency introduced by nonlinear operations, achieving a 1.65×1.65\times speedup. Taking the fully optimized hardware as the baseline, phase-aware sampling, depending on Ts​p​a​r​s​eT_{sparse}, achieves a speedup ranging from 2.31×2.31\times, 2.58×2.58\times, 2.69×2.69\times and 3.10×3.10\times, respectively, as shown in Fig. 17 (b) right. With a larger Ts​k​e​t​c​hT_{sketch}, more timesteps replace the incomplete U-Net with the complete one, and our hardware implementation achieves nearly 95%95\% of the theoretical speedup due to the highly optimized hardware implementation.

Energy Saving Analysis. As shown in Fig. 17 (c), compared to the baseline implementation, hardware optimizations achieve a 1.73×1.73\times reduction in energy consumption due to reduced latency and memory access. Additionally, phase-aware sampling further achieves a 2.63×2.63\times energy savings. It is important to note that on-chip computation energy still dominates consumption, as an FPGA consumes over 5×5\times more power than an ASIC implementation at the same process node [27]. Therefore, the energy savings would be more significant in an ASIC implementation, which we plan to explore in future work.

VI-E Comparison with SOTA Accelerators

We select the SOTA StableDiff accelerators, Cambricon-D [25] and SDP [5], for comparison. We built simulators based on the details provided in their papers to measure latency. Cambricon-D employs differential computing to optimize convolution layers by leveraging feature map similarity between consecutive timesteps. SDP utilizes prompt information to identify unimportant tokens through cross-attention computation, thereby accelerating the following FFN computation. Since Cambricon-D has the highest peak throughput, both SDP and our SD-Acc are scaled to the same peak throughput. Memory bandwidths are set to that of Cambricon-D. As shown in Fig. 18, with PAS-25/4, SD-Acc achieves a 1.8×1.8\times to 3.2×3.2\times speedup over Cambricon-D and a 1.6×1.6\times to 2.3×2.3\times speedup over SDP across three StableDiff models. This difference arises from the varying ratios of convolutions to Transformers. Transformers occupy a larger proportion in StableDiff XL, reducing Cambricon-D’s acceleration effect, while the acceleration of SDP becomes more pronounced. In contrast, our SD-Acc performs consistently well due to algorithm and hardware co-design, at the algorithmic level, phase-aware sampling skips ineffective computations in both convolution and Transformer layers, and at the hardware level, our optimizations effectively enhance the PE utilization and optimize the memory access, which puts theoretical gain into practice.

VI-F Comparison with CPU and GPU

The configurations shown in Sec. VI-B are adopted to conduct the comparison with CPU and GPU.

Energy Comparison. As shown in Fig. 19, comparing with the original model on AMD 6800H CPU (66nm), Intel 5220R CPU (1414nm), and NVIDIA V100 GPU (1212nm), our VCU118 FPGA implementation (1616nm is the least advanced process among them.) still achieves 14.7∼37.3×14.7\sim 37.3\times, 18.3∼44.9×18.3\sim 44.9\times, 2.7∼6.0×2.7\sim 6.0\times energy saving across three models. The saving mainly comes from two aspects. First, phase-aware sampling reduces both computational and memory overhead. Second, our systematic hardware optimizations effectively reduce latency, and adaptive reuse and fusion decrease off-chip accesses. It is worth noting that we choose the NVIDIA V100 GPU since it belongs to the same generation as the VCU118, and our solution is expected to achieve even greater energy savings with the ASIC implementation [27].

Speed Comparison. The NVIDIA V100 GPU has a peak throughput of 1414 TFLOPS, while our FPGA-based implementation only possesses a peak throughput of 0.20.2 TFLOPS. To make a fair comparison and keep consistent with previous accelerators [35, 42], we scale the frequency of the accelerator from 200200MHz to 11GHz and the MAC unit count from 10241024 to 40964096. As depicted in Fig. 20, for various configured three models, we achieve speedups ranging from 102.5∼258.9×102.5\sim 258.9\times, 38.4∼93.3×38.4\sim 93.3\times, and 2.2∼4.7×2.2\sim 4.7\times over the original model on AMD 6800H CPU, Intel 5220R CPU, and NVIDIA V100 GPU respectively. These speedups are achieved through algorithmic improvement, dataflow optimization, and dedicated hardware design. For the algorithm, our phase-aware sampling effectively reduces the operations, for hardware and dataflow, the address-centric dataflow and 2-stage streaming computing make the systolic array uniformly and efficiently support both convolution and attention, achieving high parallelism and hardware utilization.

VII Related Work

Diffusion Algorithm Optimizations. To accelerate the inference of diffusion models, recent efforts can be mainly classified into i) reducing denoising timesteps and ii) optimizing the architecture of U-Net. For timestep reduction, various approaches such as fast solvers, distilled models, and early stopping have been explored [34, 50, 39, 51, 37]. In terms of efficient architecture, techniques such as pruning, quantization, and knowledge distillation have been employed to enhance U-Net [10, 38, 29, 22, 30]. However, these methods don’t realize the phenomenon of phase division and overlook inference efficiency on the underlying hardware.

Phase-aware Sampling. Recently, some studies also found that the importance of each timestep varies throughout the denoising process in diffusion models [61, 44]. For example, [61] trains a slimmable network from scratch to replace the conventional U-Net, allowing the network size to adapt at each denoising timestep. Building on this, the authors propose an evolutionary algorithm to search for the optimal step-aware strategy among various candidates, suggesting that each timestep may execute a denoising network of varying sizes. However, the training and search process takes 3×3\times longer than the original training, resulting in expensive computational overhead. Similar to this idea, [44] proposes using different sizes of denoising networks for different timesteps. However, acquiring different-sized denoising networks still requires training, fine-tuning, or distillation. Moreover, these studies are based on empirical experiments but fail to uncover the underlying mechanisms. Our work uniquely demonstrates that different levels of neural network features play varying roles throughout the denoising process, revealing the significant phase-division phenomenon and showing that denoising from scratch is more computationally intensive than denoising from a sketch. Based on these observations, we propose phase-aware sampling, which can be seamlessly applied to the original U-Net, without requiring additional candidate networks, and avoids retraining or fine-tuning. By accurately targeting the source of redundancy, our solution achieves the most significant performance improvement at the lowest cost compared to these related works.

Hardware Accelerators. Various domain-specific accelerators have been designed for CNNs  [3, 4, 2, 65, 1, 19, 43] and Transformers  [58, 12, 47, 35, 62, 9]. However, while effective within their domains, Transformer accelerators are not well-suited for executing convolutional operations, and vice versa for CNN accelerators when applied to Transformers. Since StableDiff uniquely combines two distinct types of neural networks as cascaded blocks, the integration of two separate engines may result in hardware underutilization. To enable the efficient deployment of complex models on edge devices, exemplified by StableDiff, we propose effective and broadly applicable hardware optimizations, including address-centric dataflow, 2-stage streaming computing, and adaptive dataflow optimizations.

Unified Systolic Array for Linear Operators. Systolic arrays can effectively support matrix multiplications. Several works extend the original architecture with additional buses, buffers, routers, and control logic to efficiently support convolutions [3, 4, 36]. However, such extensions often introduce significant overhead, degrading both area and energy efficiency for basic matrix multiplication. Another common solution is to use im2col to transform convolution into matrix multiplication, which has seen successful deployment in both industry [31, 18] and academia [11, 26, 54, 59]. However, as reported in [11, 53], im2col in software can account for up to 30%30\% of the end-to-end latency and result in a significant increase in memory access. Placing a dedicated im2col hardware module can alleviate this issue. However, it still faces bank conflicts due to irregular memory access [53]. Additionally, frequent conversions between formats introduce explicit latency, which is further aggravated by varying feature map shapes, kernel sizes, and strides. In contrast, our address-centric dataflow offers a competitive alternative. It addresses memory irregularities and enhances PE utilization without modifying the systolic array hardware architecture, making it a nearly cost-free and effective plug-in for conventional systolic arrays.

Fusion of Nonlinear Operations. The fusion of complex nonlinear operations, such as softmax and layernorm, of Transformers has been studied in [20, 24, 7, 6]. While these works propose efficient solutions to reduce memory access and enhance the operational intensity of matrix multiplication, they do not adequately address the inherent latency of nonlinear operators. For instance, [20] does not account for the latency of softmax. As reported in [17], the softmax update operation (not complete softmax) can still consume 18.8%18.8\% of the latency in attention computation in Flash-Attention. Moreover, [24] reports that solely pursuing fusion may degrade performance, because limited buffer size could hinder the efficient tiling strategy. In contrast, our 2-stage streaming computing is proposed to solve these deficiencies systematically. It is both compatible with and orthogonal to the dataflow optimization of Flash-Attention, and it further addresses the latency issue comprehensively. It divides the nonlinear operations into two stages and integrates them into the mandatory systolic array write and read process, eliminating the need for multiple data passes. By registering only features instead of the entire data, it eliminates the need for a large buffer size. Finally, it decouples the data dependency and hides the latency in the data streaming process of the systolic array. Moreover, our reconfigurable vector processing unit uniformly supports various nonlinear operations with a single engine design without sacrificing generality or accuracy, as seen in previous approximation solutions [64, 55, 23].

Dataflow Flexible Accelerators. Existing dataflow flexible accelerators typically rely on reconfigurable on-chip networks for dataflow switching, such as [28, 46, 57]. Despite their effectiveness, the flexibility incurs high hardware overhead and bandwidth demands. SD-Acc proposes a compromise solution: At the SA-to-buffer level, it adopts a fixed address-centric dataflow to unify Convolution and Matmul computations, minimizing the overhead increment of SA. At the buffer-to-memory level, specifically tailored for StableDiff, it employs adaptive dataflow optimization to reduce off-chip access, which is a major contributor to energy consumption [56].

VIII Conclusion

This paper proposes a novel approach to accelerate StableDiff via algorithm and hardware co-optimizations. By investigating the statistics of StableDiff, this work proposes a novel phase-aware sampling, which adaptively applies approxiate computation through an optimization framework without harming the image quality. To accelerate the models with multiple distinct operators, we propose an address-centric dataflow, 2-stage streaming computing, and adaptive dataflow optimization, significantly improving the hardware performance and efficiency. Combining both algorithm and hardware optimizations, our solution achieves 2.7∼6.0×2.7\sim 6.0\times higher energy efficiency than the NVIDIA GPU implementation.
